setting: a language-learning marketplace connecting tutors and students (Lingua Bridge)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for Priya Patel, our CEO, about rolling out a “Live Group Class” feature on Lingua Bridge. The idea is to let tutors run 90‑minute group sessions for up to 8 students, priced at $25 per student per hour. We estimate that each tutor could fill 4 groups per week, generating an extra $800 weekly per tutor (8 students × $25 × 1.5 hrs × 4). We have 400 active tutors, so the projected incremental revenue is $320,000 per month, a 15 % lift over our current $2.1 M monthly revenue. The development cost is $120,000, plus $80,000 for marketing, and we plan a 3‑month pilot starting 1 Oct 2024. I’m assuming that 70 % of tutors will adopt the format within the first month. The unknown is the actual student uptake—how many will sign up for group classes versus one‑on‑one sessions. I need you to give Priya one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us halt the rollout (e.g., if the pilot’s net revenue contribution falls below a certain threshold). Please also watch for any hidden cost or risk I may have missed.

setting: a regional bank's small-business lending team (Harbor Trust)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the “Rapid Expansion” proposal I’m taking to our Chief Lending Officer, Maya Patel, next week. Harbor Trust’s small‑business loan book is $12 million as of 31 Mar 2025 and we’re targeting a 15 % growth by Dec 2025. The plan calls for opening five new branches in the Metro area, hiring 12 loan officers (a 30 % increase in staff overhead) and investing $200 k per branch in technology upgrades, for a total outlay of $1.2 million. We assume interest rates will stay flat through the year and that our current underwriting capacity can handle the extra volume without additional compliance staff. The unknown is the adoption rate of the new “instant‑approve” product the regional fintech competitor launched in June 2024; we have no hard data on how quickly small businesses will switch. I want you to give Maya one clear recommendation (go ahead, modify, or hold), list the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us abort the plan (e.g., if net new loan volume falls short of X by Q3). Note that the projected $2 million revenue gain is based on a simple 15 % of $12 million calculation, which may be off. Please flag any hidden costs, regulatory risks, or flawed assumptions. Thanks.

setting: a county public library digital-services group (Alder County Library)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for the digital‑services team at Alder County Library and need it stress‑tested before I present it to our Library Director, Ms. Fiona Hart. We have a $120,000 annual digital budget and want to allocate $85,000 to launch a new e‑book platform that would add 1,600 titles (bringing our catalog from 2,400 to 4,000). I’ve budgeted a three‑month pilot at $25,000 per month, or $70,000 total, leaving a $15,000 cushion for contingencies. My assumption is that at least 30 % of our 12,000 registered patrons will adopt the service within the first year, generating a 15 % lift in overall digital checkouts. We plan to start the pilot on June 1 2025 and expect results by September 1 2025. The unknown is the licensing terms for the popular “Chronicles of Alder” series, which could add an extra cost we haven’t priced. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the main ways this rollout could fail (including any hidden risks you spot), and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would trigger us to kill the project. The answer is for Ms. Hart, who will decide based on the risk/benefit trade‑off.

setting: a B2B cybersecurity training vendor (Redoak Secure)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the rollout plan I’m about to present to our COO, Maya Patel, at Redoak Secure. We want to add a microlearning “Phishing‑Resistant Culture” add‑on to our existing platform. The numbers we’ve built into the business case are: a 12‑month pilot with 5 existing enterprise clients, each paying $150,000, which should generate $750,000 in pilot revenue; we estimate development costs of $500,000 and a marketing push of $120,000. We assume 80 % of our current 120 customers will cross‑sell to the add‑on, giving us a $9.6 M opportunity in year 2. Our target adoption rate among pilot users is 30 % and we forecast churn of 15 % in the first year. The only unknown is how long it will take to produce the EU‑GDPR compliance content, which could add extra effort. I want you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the three most likely ways the plan could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot – specifically if the pilot Net‑Promoter Score drops below 30 or the ROI after six months is under 12 %. Please also point out any arithmetic slip or flawed comparison you see in the figures.

setting: an indie game studio with one hit title (Moth Lantern Games)
prompt: I’m pitching a shift to the new “Aether” engine for our upcoming DLC to Maya Patel, our CTO, and I need it stress‑tested before the board meeting on 14 May 2025. Our current Unity license is $150 k per year, and the Aether license is a one‑time $300 k. We estimate the switch will cut development from 8 months to 6 months, saving roughly $200 k in staff costs (12 engineers at $100 k each for two months). Training the team will cost about $100 k, so I’m telling the board the net increase is $300 k + $100 k – $200 k = $500 k (actually $400 k). I’m assuming the new engine reduces iteration bugs by 30 % and that the faster cycle will let us release the DLC on 1 Dec 2025 instead of the original 15 Jan 2026. The real unknown is the exact licensing fee for the third‑party physics middleware we’ll need to integrate, which the vendor only quotes as “around $30k–$45k.” I need you to give Maya one recommendation, list the main ways this plan could fail (technical integration, cost overruns, timeline slip, etc.), and specify the pre‑agreed condition—if the total cost exceeds $450 k or the release slips past 31 Dec 2025, we’ll kill the switch.

setting: a home-solar installer expanding to a second state (Sunrow Energy)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to take Sunrow Energy into Texas and need it stress‑tested before I bring it to Maya Patel, our CEO. Right now we do $4.2 M in revenue in Arizona with $2.5 M of operating costs, giving a 40 % gross margin. The plan calls for hiring three new installers (each at $85 k salary), buying $500 k of inventory, and spending $150 k on state licensing and permitting. We estimate we can close 250 residential solar installs in the first 12 months at an average contract price of $32 k, which would generate $8 M in revenue. I’m assuming the Texas solar incentive of 30 % will remain unchanged for the next three years, and I’m comparing our current per‑kilowatt cost of $2.5 k in Arizona to a published $2.0 k per kW in Texas without adjusting for the higher labor rates we’ve seen in Dallas. The unknown is the exact permitting timeline per county, which could add weeks to each job. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the main ways this rollout could fail, and specify the result (e.g., net margin dropping below 5 % after the first year) that would trigger us to stop or rethink the expansion.

setting: a dental practice management software vendor (Brightsmile Systems)
prompt: I need a quick stress test of the “SmartSchedule” rollout before I pitch it to our CEO, Jane Doe, on Thursday. The plan is to invest $450,000 in development and $200,000 in marketing, then launch a 90‑day pilot starting July 1 2024 with three of our top clinics (each handling ~1,200 appointments per month). We expect a 30 % drop in no‑show rates, which should lift monthly revenue by about $66,000 per clinic (based on our average $220 per appointment). Over the first 18 months we’re projecting $1.2 million in incremental revenue. The assumption is that 70 % of our existing 120 customers will adopt the module within six months of release. The unknown is how many new dental practices will sign up because of this feature; we have no data on that market pull. I want you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways the rollout could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the project (e.g., adoption below a certain level or cost overrun). Also note any hidden risks I haven’t covered.

setting: a university alumni-donations office (Kestrel University Advancement)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for Karen Liu, our VP of Development, and need it stress‑tested before I present it at the leadership meeting on 12 Nov 2026. The plan is to launch a “Class‑Together” giving drive for alumni who graduated between 2000 and 2020, using a 2:1 matching grant from the Kestrel Foundation. The prior “Centennial” campaign in 2022 raised $800 k on a $200 k spend, and we’re assuming a linear scale to justify the larger budget. The unknown is the actual response rate for the social‑media component, which we haven’t tested. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, identify the main ways this could fail (including any arithmetic slip, unexamined assumption, or missing cost), and state the specific result that would trigger us to kill the initiative (e.g., ROI dropping below a 1.5 : 1 ratio after three months).

setting: a meal-kit company for athletes (Ironplate Meals)
prompt:
I’m drafting a proposal to take to our CEO, Jordan Kim, and I need it stress‑tested before the board meeting on 3 May 2025. The idea is to launch a “Performance Pack” line of Ironplate Meals for elite athletes, priced at $25 per box, delivered weekly. We project 8,000 subscribers by month 12, generating $2 million in revenue (8,000 × $25 × 12 = $2 M) with an assumed gross margin of 20% after a $0.30 per‑box packaging cost. I’m assuming churn will be 5% per month, but we have no data on how many of our existing 22,000 customers will actually upgrade, which is the real unknown. I also expect the new refrigerated trucks to reduce delivery time by 15 minutes, which I think will boost retention, but I haven’t priced the additional fuel surcharge of roughly $0.08 per mile.

Please give me one clear recommendation for Jordan, list the main ways this plan could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., churn exceeding X % or margin dropping below Y %) that would trigger us to stop or pivot the initiative.

setting: a legal-document automation startup for solo lawyers (Clause & Co)
prompt: I’m pulling together a pitch for Maya, our co‑founder, about launching a premium “Document Builder Pro” package for solo lawyers. The market research says there are roughly 150 solo practitioners in our target metro area, and we expect a 30 % conversion from the free tier within six months of launch (by 30 Sep 2024). The premium tier would cost $15 k per year, giving us an estimated $675 k ARR if the conversion holds (150 × 0.30 × $15 k). We’ve budgeted $120 k for additional API licensing, $45 k for a one‑off UI redesign, and $30 k for marketing spend in Q4 2024, assuming each solo lawyer will spend about 3 hours per month on the tool. I’m also assuming our current support staff can handle a 50 % increase in tickets without extra hires. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to push this forward, outline the three biggest ways the rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the project (e.g., a threshold for monthly recurring revenue or adoption rate).

setting: a hospital outpatient scheduling team (St. Mara Outpatient)
prompt: I'm about to pitch a new centralized scheduling hub for St. Mara Outpatient to Dr. Evelyn Grant, our COO. The hub would consolidate the three current scheduling desks into a single location, add two full‑time triage nurses, and replace the legacy software with a cloud‑based system that costs $250,000 upfront plus $30,000 per year. We currently handle 120 appointments per day, with a 15% no‑show rate that costs roughly $45,000 monthly. The proposal assumes the new nurses will cut the no‑show rate by 20%, saving $9,000 per month, and that the cloud platform will improve booking speed by 25% without any integration downtime. The unknown is how the change will affect patient satisfaction scores, which we have not measured for a similar rollout. I need you to give Dr. Grant one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and specify the exact metric or condition that would make us kill the project after the first quarter. The deadline for the memo is 15 Oct 2024.

setting: a fleet-electrification consultancy (Voltway Advisors)
prompt: Hi, I'm Alex, head of the vehicle transition team at Voltway Advisors. I need a concise brief for Maya Patel, the CFO of Harbor Logistics, who will decide whether we move forward with our 24‑month electric‑van rollout. The plan is to replace 120 medium‑duty delivery vans, starting June 1 2024 and completing by Dec 31 2025. We estimate an upfront capital outlay of $1.2 million and project 12,500 miles per van per year, which we mistakenly summed to 1.5 million total miles (the correct figure is 1.8 million). We assume electricity stays at $0.12/kWh and that battery degradation is limited to 5 % per year, but we have not priced the replacement of modules after two years. Fuel cost is currently $3.80 /gal, though forecasts show it could fall to $2.90 /gal by Q3 2025. The state rebate is rumored to be $200 k, but the exact schedule is still unknown. I need one recommendation on whether to pitch this, the three biggest ways the proposal could fail, and the pre‑agreed kill condition – for example, if the total cost of ownership exceeds the diesel baseline by more than 8 %. Please tailor the answer for Maya.

setting: an HR analytics platform sold to mid-size manufacturers (Peoplegrid)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the plan I’m taking to Maya Patel, our CTO, next week. Peoplegrid wants to launch a predictive turnover module for mid‑size manufacturers. The development budget is $250,000, we’ve allocated six months (starting 1 Oct 2026) for engineering, and we expect a rollout to 15 pilot sites by 31 Mar 2027. The business case assumes a 12% reduction in employee turnover, which should lift our average contract value from $45,000 to $50,500 per client – a $5,500 uplift per contract. We’re also assuming manufacturers will integrate the API with their ERP systems in two weeks, and that at least 30% of users will adopt the new dashboard within the first quarter. The unknown is how long data‑cleaning will actually take once we get raw HR logs from each plant; early estimates range from one to three weeks per site. I also realized we didn’t factor in an extra $30,000 for third‑party data‑validation services, which could push the total cost over $280,000. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to push ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the pre‑agreed kill condition (e.g., if ROI after 12 months is below 8% or adoption stays under 15%).

setting: a podcast hosting and ad-marketplace company (Echolane)
prompt: Maya, I need your help stress‑testing a proposal I’m taking to our CEO, Maya Patel, next week. The plan is to roll out a dynamic ad‑insertion engine on the Echolane platform starting 15 August 2025. We expect to serve 2.3 million monthly listeners and think the new engine will lift CPM from $20 to $22.40 – that’s a 12 % increase, which we’re assuming holds across all genres. The budget we’ve allocated is $500 k for development and $150 k per month for additional hosting, and we’ve projected an extra $300 k in ad revenue in the first six months. We’ve also set a goal of a 8 % conversion from free to premium listeners, up from the current 4 %. The unknown is how the new pricing tier will affect churn – we have no hard data on that. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push ahead, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., if net profit after month 3 falls below $50 k). Note that we haven’t factored the cost of additional content moderation required by higher ad volume. Thanks.

setting: a veterinary clinic chain (Pawprint Vets)
prompt: I need a quick stress test of a rollout plan I’m taking to Maya Patel, our COO, next week. Pawprint Vets currently operates 12 clinics, each pulling roughly $180,000 in monthly revenue (about $2.16 M total). We want to open three new locations in the Tri‑City area, each with an estimated build‑out and equipment cost of $500,000, slated for Q3 2025. The business case assumes a 15% boost in client retention from our new loyalty program, which we think will lift average monthly revenue per clinic by $30,000. We also plan to integrate a cloud‑based scheduling platform; the vendor quoted $45,000 for licensing but we haven’t received the exact integration and training cost yet (real unknown). My assumption is that the new sites will break even after 18 months because we expect a 20% drop in no‑show rates, though we haven’t modeled the staffing ramp‑up expense. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways this could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the project (e.g., if break‑even moves beyond 24 months). Note that I’ve added the three new clinics’ revenue as $540,000 per month, which you may want to double‑check.

setting: an online used-furniture marketplace (Second Seat)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to take to our CEO, Maya Patel, about expanding Second Seat’s “Pickup‑Only” model into three new regional hubs—Cedar Creek, Oakridge, and Pine Hollow—starting Q3 2025. The plan assumes we can convert 30 % of our current 12 month online order volume (about 18,000 units) to pickup, which we estimate will save $2 million in last‑mile delivery costs and increase gross margin by roughly 5 percentage points. The budget we’ve allocated is $1.2 million for lease, staffing, and equipment, and we expect the hubs to break even after 10 months based on a projected 8 % month‑over‑month growth in pickup orders. One key assumption is that the average sale price will stay at $150, and that our existing warehouse space can absorb the additional inventory without extra handling fees. The unknown is how the new hubs will affect our overall delivery network capacity, especially during peak weekend demand, which we haven’t modeled. Please give me a single recommendation on whether to move forward, list the principal ways this rollout could fail, and specify the concrete result (e.g., a sustained 15 % higher than expected delivery delay or a $250 k cost overrun) that would trigger us to kill or radically change the plan.

setting: a construction-bid estimating tool (Cornerstone Bids)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for the CFO, Maya Patel, to adopt Cornerstone Bids for our estimating workflow at Rivermont Builders. Right now our average estimate variance is 8% on a portfolio of ten $5 million projects per year, which costs us roughly $4 million in change orders annually. Cornerstone claims it can bring variance down to 5%, which we’ve modeled as a $150 000 annual saving (3% × $5 million × 10). The license is $45 000 plus $12 000 for a two‑day onsite training, and we’d need a six‑week rollout. I’m assuming we can integrate the tool with our ERP in three weeks, but the data‑migration effort is unknown. The vendor lists a 99.9 % cloud uptime, yet there’s no SLA on support response times. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, identify the main ways this could fail (e.g., integration delays, under‑estimated migration cost, hidden subscription fees of $8 000/year, or the tool’s limited multi‑phase project handling), and state the condition under which we would kill the plan—specifically if after three months the variance reduction is less than 2 percentage points. Also point out the strongest objection we might hear and, if there’s a better alternative, outline it.

setting: a wine-subscription direct-to-consumer brand (Vinelet)
prompt: Maya Patel, our COO, wants a quick stress test before I present the “Reserve Club” tier to the board next week. Here’s what we have: Vinelet currently serves 12,000 subscribers at an average $45 per month, giving us $540,000 in monthly revenue. Our churn is 3% per quarter and we assume the new tier will have the same churn rate. The plan is to add 5,000 “Reserve Club” members by Q3 2025, each paying $70 per month for six premium bottles. We’ll spend $120,000 on a targeted Instagram campaign and $30,000 on a limited‑edition packaging redesign. The cost to us is $8 per bottle, but we’re counting a $2 shipping subsidy per order that we haven’t factored into the margin calculation yet. The expected contribution margin is projected at 30%, which would lift quarterly profit by $405,000. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., subscriber acquisition cost > $25 per new member or churn rising above 5% in the first two months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the idea. The real unknown is how seasonal shipping delays will affect churn. Thanks.

setting: a city transit agency's rider-information app team (Metro Line Digital)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the “Live‑Crowd Density” add‑on I’m about to pitch to Maya Patel, our COO, next week. The plan is to pull anonymized Bluetooth beacon data from the city’s new sensor network and layer it on our Metro Line app to show real‑time crowding on each train car. We’ve budgeted $2.5 million for development, $500 k for the first year of licensing, and we expect a rollout in 12 months. Our current app serves 3.2 million daily riders; the business case assumes an 8 % lift in ridership (≈256 k extra rides per day) and a $0.78 per‑ride revenue bump, which should cover the cost in under two years. I’m assuming we can get the city’s data‑sharing agreement signed by Q2 and that integration with our backend will take no more than 4 weeks. The unknown is the API latency from the sensor provider – we only have a vague “under 500 ms” estimate. I want you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and the specific metric or result that would trigger us to kill the project according to the pre‑agreed condition (e.g., if the ridership lift falls short of a threshold after six months). Please keep the answer focused on Maya’s decision.

setting: a developer-tools company selling a CI accelerator (Quickbuild)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test a proposal I’m taking to our CTO, Maya Patel, next week. Quickbuild currently serves 200 paying customers, 15 % of whom are enterprise accounts that together generate $630 k of our $4.2 M annual revenue. Our monthly churn sits at 7 % and we’ve set a target to drop it to 4 % within six months by improving build performance. Development will take three months, after which we’ll roll it out as an optional add‑on priced at $9 per seat per month. The unknown is how many existing customers will actually adopt the add‑on; we estimate 30 % uptake, but we have no survey data. Also, the competitor’s similar offering costs $12 per seat but includes unlimited builds, a factor we haven’t fully compared. Please give me one clear recommendation, the main ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., adoption below X % or cost overruns over $150 k) that would trigger us to kill or rethink the project.

setting: a K-12 school-district software vendor (Maple Learning Systems)
prompt: I’m drafting a pitch for Maya Patel, our CEO, about moving Maple Learning Systems’ flagship student‑information platform to a micro‑services cloud architecture. The plan is to start the migration on 15 January 2025, finish in 9 months, and retire the legacy monolith that currently costs us $350 k per year in licensing and $120 k in on‑site support. setting: an insurance broker adding a self-serve quote tool (Anchor Mutual Brokers)

The plan is to develop the web widget over a 90‑day sprint starting 15 Oct 2024, with an estimated budget of $220,000 for design, API integration, and QA. setting: a regional grocery delivery startup (Tidewater Fresh)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for our CEO, Raj Singh, to switch Tidewater Fresh’s last‑mile routing from our current in‑house algorithm to a third‑party SaaS platform. The contract is $500 k per year, with a 12‑month minimum, and the vendor claims a 15 % reduction in average delivery time based on a pilot in a neighboring market that handled 30 % more orders (2,600 vs. 2,000 per week). setting: a payroll software company for small restaurants (Acme Payroll)

The idea is to bundle our core payroll module (currently $99 per month per location) with a lightweight inventory tracker we built last year. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you see), and the specific metric or result that would trigger us to kill the project or pivot. Thanks.

setting: a pediatric telehealth clinic network (Northwind Kids Health)
prompt: I’m preparing a briefing for Dr. Maya Patel, our Chief Medical Officer, about rolling out an AI‑driven triage chatbot for Northwind Kids Health. We currently handle about 150,000 pediatric visits per year, generating $2.5 million in revenue. The plan calls for a phased launch in Q3 2024, with a target of 30 % of families using the bot by Q1 2025. We’ve budgeted $300,000 for development, $150,000 for integration, and $50,000 for training, which I summed to $500,000, but I’m not sure I haven’t missed any recurring licensing fees. The assumption is that at least 25 % of parents will opt in once we market the feature, based on a survey of 200 households. The unknown is how long regulatory clearance will take—estimates range from three to nine months, and we have no firm timeline. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward now, outline the main ways this could fail (e.g., adoption shortfall, data‑privacy breach, cost overruns), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us pull the plug or pivot (e.g., if adoption stays below 10 % after six months or if regulatory sign‑off exceeds six months).

setting: a 40-person logistics software company selling to freight brokers (Brightline Freight)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to present to Maya Patel, our COO, about replacing our in‑house routing engine with a third‑party SaaS platform. Right now the custom engine costs us $120,000 per year in licensing and maintenance, and it supports an average of 4,500 load assignments per month. The SaaS option is priced at $15,000 per month, but promises a 12% reduction in average route distance, which we estimate could save about $210,000 annually in fuel and driver overtime. I’m assuming the integration will take six weeks of developer time (≈ 480 hours) and that our existing API will map cleanly onto the SaaS API. The contract would be for 24 months, with a 3‑month opt‑out window. The unknown is the provider’s guaranteed uptime and any hidden data‑migration fees; they claim 99.9% uptime but have no public SLA. I need a single recommendation on whether to move forward, the three most likely ways this switch could fail (technical, financial, or operational), and the specific result—such as a net cost increase of more than 5% after the first year or a downtime event lasting longer than four hours—that would trigger us to cancel or postpone the plan.

setting: a consumer budgeting app with a free tier (Pennywise)
prompt: I’m preparing to pitch a new “Pennywise Premium” tier to our CFO, Maya Patel, and I need the plan stress‑tested before the board meeting on 15 Nov 2024. Right now we have 520 k active free users, generating $1.2 M in ad revenue last year with a 30 % annual churn. The proposal is to roll out a premium subscription at $4.99/month, aiming for 3 % conversion of the current free base within 12 months, which we estimate will add $800 k in ARR. We assume the development effort will cost $400 k and that the existing support team can absorb the extra tickets without additional headcount. I’ve also added a projected $150 k marketing boost, but I haven’t factored any cost for the new payment gateway integration, which we still don’t know the price of. The financial model shows total revenue climbing from $1.2 M to $2.0 M, but I realize I added $800 k to $1.2 M incorrectly—it should be $2.0 M only if churn stays at 30 % and no users drop out. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the main ways this could fail (including the hidden integration cost and the churn assumption), and tell me the specific result (e.g., conversion below 1.5 % after six months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the idea.

setting: an industrial sensor maker moving into subscriptions (Ferrous Sensing)
prompt: Maya Patel, our CFO, will be reviewing the subscription push next week and I need a quick stress‑test before the deck goes out. Ferrous Sensing has $12 M in annual hardware sales, and we’re proposing a data‑analytics subscription that should bring $8 M in ARR in the first year (ramping to $15 M in year 2). The rollout is slated for Q3 2025, with a pilot of 150 key OEM customers starting January 2025. We’re budgeting $4 M to build the analytics platform and have assumed a 30 % conversion rate of our existing OEM base, which currently numbers 2,000 installed sensor sites. Our model uses a processing cost of $0.12 per reading, but we originally entered $0.10 in the spreadsheet; at the forecasted 100 M readings per year that’s a $2 M difference. We’re also assuming a 5 % annual churn and that hardware renewal contracts will stay flat (the exact renewal rate is still unknown). Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three most likely ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result or metric that would trigger us to kill the plan or pivot. The answer is for Maya Patel.
